entries.seminar_title: The Garden as Common Ground: Food Justice, Climate, and Peacebuilding
entries.speaker: See Abstract
Vincent Chartray
entries.abstract: This paper investigates how trade policy is reflected in asset prices and quantifies the risk premium associated with trade policy uncertainty. To do so, I exploit exposure to trade policy uncertainty arising from Congressional votes to revoke China's preferential tariff treatment between 1990 and 2001. A portfolio isolating exposure to trade policy uncertainty earns an 8.3% annual risk premium. This effect is greater in sectors less protected from globalization and more dependent on inputs from China. I discuss conditions under which a model of trade with asset prices can explain the effects of tariffs and trade policy uncertainty on asset prices and the risk premium.

entries.seminar_title: Public-Sector Pay, Worker Selection, and Government Performance: Evidence from Locality Pay Areas in the U.S.
entries.speaker: Diego Tocre
entries.abstract: How does geographically differentiated public-sector pay affect the composition and performance of the federal workforce? We study the creation and expansion of Locality Pay Areas (LPAs), geographic zones where federal salaries are raised to keep pace with local private-sector wages across U.S. labor markets. Leveraging staggered county-level variation in LPA adoption and administrative payroll data, we find that federal employment in the average treated county rises 14% within seven years, an implied labor-supply elasticity near two. Growth is concentrated in occupations with strong private-sector outside options, and comes from relocating incumbent federal workers out of the urban core rather than new hires. We find no effect on service contracting.

entries.seminar_title: Peer Earnings Disclosure at Work: Evidence from Two Field Experiments (JMP)
entries.speaker: Zhi Hao Lim
entries.abstract: I study how recurring peer earnings disclosure affects labor supply in performance-based work using two field experiments with over 3,000 ride-hailing drivers. During each six-week intervention, all drivers received twice-weekly updates on their own cumulative earnings; I randomized whether these updates also reported the average earnings of their reference group of ten similar drivers. An incentivized measure of drivers' demand for peer information, elicited at baseline, identifies the same responsive worker type in both experiments nearly one year apart. The response to peer earnings information, however, reverses: information-seeking drivers increase total platform hours by 6% in the first experiment through greater work intensity but reduce them by 5% in the second through lower platform participation. Non-information-seeking drivers show no detectable response in either experiment. By contrast, both types respond similarly to randomized monetary incentives. I develop a model in which peer earnings convey both relative-performance and common market-opportunity information. Consistent with market learning, peer-information effects become more positive when market conditions are unexpectedly favorable. A decomposition exercise suggests that differences in market conditions can account for over 40% of the cross-experiment reversal. The findings show that information demand predicts who responds to peer earnings disclosure, while the economic content embedded in peer outcomes helps explain how they respond.

entries.seminar_title: Local Asymptotics for Treatment Choice with Partial Identification
entries.speaker: Jörg Stoye
entries.abstract: We provide a new asymptotic framework to derive approximately optimal treatment assignments when sampling noise from data is compounded by fundamental uncertainty due to partial identification. We recenter the reduced-form parameter around its 	least-favorable	 configuration and consider drifting parameter sequences that yield both diminishing levels of sampling uncertainty and of partial identification. We characterize the limiting decision problem as a normal location shift model with a suitable limiting identified set. We apply our results to treatment choice problems with contaminated outcomes, to robust welfare analyses with partially identified consumer surplus, and to the problem of aggregating experimental estimates for policy adoption.

entries.seminar_title: Cooperation and Common-Pool Resources in Mean Field Games and Extensions to Inverse Learning
entries.speaker: Gökçe Dayanıklı
entries.abstract: The tragedy of the commons (TOTC) states that individual incentives lead to the overuse of common-pool resources (CPRs), potentially resulting in detrimental future consequences for everyone. However, TOTC does not occur in many real-life settings, and researchers such as Nobel laureate Elinor Ostrom have suggested that mutual restraint by individuals can prevent it. In mean field games (MFGs), individuals are insignificant and non‑cooperative, making TOTC inevitable. This suggests that MFG models involving CPRs must incorporate both selfishness and altruism to better capture real‑world behavior. Motivated by this observation, we introduce new classes of models, mixed MFGs, and use the probabilistic approach to analyze equilibrium notions blending cooperative and non‑cooperative actions. We then present a fisheries‑inspired example and discuss theoretical and experimental results. Finally, we address the challenge that understanding intervention policies in mixed MFGs requires knowledge of individuals’ altruism levels, which are generally unobservable. We therefore establish how these levels can be learned from data using inverse learning techniques.
entries.bio: Gökçe Dayanıklı is an Assistant Professor of Economics at Columbia University. Her research interests are in game theory, microeconomic theory, and applied probability. She received her PhD in Economics from Princeton University in 2021.

entries.seminar_title: Satisficing Regret Minimization in Bandits: Constant Bound and Light-Tailed Distribution
entries.speaker: Prof. Ruihao Zhu
entries.affiliation: Cornell SC Johnson College of Business
entries.abstract: Motivated by the concept of satisficing in decision-making, we consider the problem of satisficing regret minimization in bandit optimization. In this setting, the learner aims at selecting satisficing arms (arms with mean reward exceeding a certain threshold value) as frequently as possible. The performance is measured by satisficing regret, which is the cumulative deficit of the chosen arm's mean reward compared to the threshold. We propose SELECT, a general algorithmic template for Satisficing Regret Minimization via Sampling and Lower Confidence bound Testing, that attains constant expected satisficing regret for a wide variety of bandit optimization problems in the realizable case (i.e., a satisficing arm exists). Specifically, given a class of bandit optimization problems and a corresponding learning oracle with sub-linear expected (standard) regret upper bound, SELECT iteratively makes use of the oracle to identify a potential satisficing arm with low regret. Then, it collects data samples from this arm, and continuously compares the LCB of the identified arm's mean reward against the threshold value to determine if it is a satisficing arm. As a complement, SELECT also enjoys the same (standard) regret guarantee as the oracle in the non-realizable case. To further ensure stability of the algorithm, we introduce SELECT-LITE that achieves a light-tailed satisficing regret distribution plus a constant expected satisficing regret in the realizable case and a sub-linear expected (standard) regret in the non-realizable case. Notably, SELECT-LITE can operate on learning oracles with heavy-tailed (standard) regret distribution. More importantly, our results reveal the surprising compatibility between constant expected satisficing regret and light-tailed satisficing regret distribution, which is in sharp contrast to the case of (standard) regret. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to validate the performance of SELECT and SELECT-LITE on both synthetic datasets and a real-world dynamic pricing case study.
entries.bio: Ruihao Zhu (https://rzhu.github.io/) is an Assistant Professor at the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business. He designs agents for the digital economy and revenue management. Ruihao’s research has received several recognitions, including the POMS Early Career Award (2nd place) and the INFORMS Innovative Applications in Analytics Award (2nd place).

entries.seminar_title: Volterra clocks and their singular limits: hitting times of curved boundaries
entries.speaker: Prof. Andreas Sojmark
entries.abstract: In this talk, I will introduce Volterra clocks, a new class of continuous non-decreasing processes whose affine case recovers the integrated Volterra square-root process. Via a time-changed Brownian representation, we develop a simple framework for functional convergence which allows us to study their singular limits as the memory kernels collapse to a Dirac mass. Specifically, the clocks degenerate into pure-jump processes given by first-passage times of Brownian motion to curved boundaries. Moreover, the rate bursts producing each jump are resolved through a `decorated' notion of convergence which goes beyond any of the Skorokhod topologies.
entries.bio: Andreas Sojmark is an Assistant Professor at the Department of Statistics at Columbia University. His research interests include stochastic processes, statistical physics, and financial mathematics.

entries.seminar_title: A complete generalization of Kelly betting
entries.speaker: Prof. Aaditya Ramdas
entries.abstract:
In the 1950s, John Kelly (working at Bell Labs like Claude Shannon) fundamentally connected gambling on coin tosses with Shannon's information theory, and this was soon extended by Leo Breiman (1963) to more general settings. In an excellent 1999 Yale PhD thesis, Jonathan Li defined and studied a concept called the reverse information projection (RIPr), which is a Kullback-Leibler projection of a given probability measure onto a given set of probability measures. Grunwald et al. (2024) showed that the RIPr characterizes the log-optimal bet/e-variable of a point alternative hypothesis against a composite null hypothesis, albeit under several assumptions (convexity, absolute continuity, etc). In this talk, we will show how to fully and completely generalize the theory underlying Kelly betting and the RIPr, showing that the RIPr is always well defined, without *any* assumptions. Further, a strong duality result identifies it as the dual to an optimal bet/e-variable called the numeraire, which is unique and also always exists without assumptions. This fully generalizes classical Kelly betting to arbitrary composite nulls; the same assumptionless strong duality also holds for Renyi/Hellinger projections (replacing the logarithmic utility by power utilities).
The talk will not assume any prior knowledge on these topics. This is joint work with Martin Larsson and Johannes Ruf (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18810), and appeared in the Annals of Statistics (2025).
entries.bio: Aaditya Ramdas is a tenured Associate Professor at Carnegie Mellon University in the Departments of Statistics and Machine Learning. His work has been recognized by the Presidential Early Career Award (PECASE), the highest distinction bestowed by the US government to young scientists, a Kavli fellowship from the NAS, a Sloan fellowship in Mathematics, a CAREER award from the NSF, the inaugural COPSS Emerging Leader Award, the Bernoulli new researcher award and the IMS Peter Hall Early Career Prize, and faculty research awards from Adobe and Google. Aaditya was recently elected Fellow of the IMS, was awarded Statistician of the Year by the ASA's Pittsburgh Chapter, and is the program chair of AISTATS 2026. He won a best thesis award for his PhD at CMU in 2015 after obtaining his undergraduate degree in computer science at IIT Bombay, recently receiving a Young Alumnus Achiever Award.

entries.seminar_title: Efficient sampling with diffusion models: Sharp and adaptive guarantees
entries.speaker: Prof. Yuting Wei
entries.abstract: The score-based diffusion models have become a cornerstone of modern generative AI. While recent works aim to develop sharp convergence guarantees, the iteration complexity of existing analyses typically scales with the ambient data dimension $d$ of the target distribution, leading to overly conservative theory that fails to explain its practical efficiency. This motivates us to understand how diffusion models can achieve sampling speed-ups through automatic exploitation of intrinsic low dimensionality of data for both continuous and discrete distributions. This talk explores two key scenarios: (1) For a broad class of continuous distributions with intrinsic dimension $k$, we show that the iteration complexity of the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) scales nearly linearly with $k$, which is optimal under the KL divergence metric; (2) For masking discrete diffusions, under a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) formulation, we introduce a modified $	au$-leaping sampler whose convergence rate is governed by an intrinsic information-theoretic quantity, termed the effective total correlation, which is upper bounded by $d 	extrm{log} S$ (with $S$ the vocabulary size) but can be sublinear or even constant for structured discrete distributions.
entries.bio: Dr. Yuting Wei is an Associate Professor in the Statistics and Data Science Department at the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania. Prior to that, Dr. Wei spent two years at Carnegie Mellon University as an assistant professor and one year at Stanford University as a Stein's Fellow. She received her Ph.D. in statistics at the University of California, Berkeley. She was the recipient of the 2025 Gottfried E. Noether Early Career Scholar Award, Google Research Scholar Award, NSF Career award, and the Erich L. Lehmann Citation from the Berkeley statistics department. Her research interests include high-dimensional and non-parametric statistics, reinforcement learning, and diffusion models.

entries.seminar_title: Fluctuations Around the Mean-Field Limit for Attractive Riesz Interaction Kernels in the Moderate Regime
entries.speaker: Prof. Alexandra Holzinger
entries.abstract: In this talk we will give a short introduction to moderately interacting particle systems and the general notion of fluctuations around the mean-field limit. We will see how a central limit theorem can be shown for moderately interacting particles on the whole space for certain types of interaction potentials. The interaction potential approximates singular attractive potentials of sub-Coulomb type and we can show that the fluctuations become asymptotically Gaussians. The methodology is inspired by the classical work of Oelschläger in the 1980s on fluctuations for the porous-medium equation. To allow for attractive potentials we use a new approach of quantitative mean-field convergence in probability in order to include aggregation effects. This is joint work with Li Chen and Ansgar Jüngel.
entries.bio: Alexandra Holzinger is an Assistant Professor of Mathematics at Columbia University. Her research interests lie in the mathematical analysis of systems of interacting particles, with a focus on stochastic processes and PDEs.

entries.seminar_title: Mean field control with absorption or stopping.
entries.speaker: Joe Jackson
entries.abstract: Mean field control (MFC) theory deals with stochastic control problems in which a large number of agents work together to minimize a symmetric cost functional. In ongoing joint work with Cardaliaguet and Souganidis, we consider two variants of MFC in which the total number of agents in the system can change over time. In the first case, each agents' state process evolves in a bounded domain, and an agent is removed from the system if its state process reaches the boundary. In the second case, the agents can choose to exit the system voluntarily at any moment by paying a fee. For both problems, we obtain convergence of the value functions as N \to \infty by proving a comparison principle for the infinite-dimensional partial differential equation which describes the value of the limiting optimization problem.
entries.bio: Joe Jackson is a Postdoctoral Research Fellow at Columbia University. His research focuses on stochastic control, mean-field games, and partial differential equations.

entries.seminar_title: The Geometry of Adapted Optimal Transport
entries.speaker: Prof. Beatrice Acciaio
entries.abstract: The adapted Wasserstein distance has been proven to be a suitable metric for comparing stochastic processes while accounting for their temporal structure, especially in a context of model uncertainty in finance. In this talk I will present our study of the geometry of the adapted Wasserstein space of stochastic processes. We provide a probabilistic representation of absolutely continuous curves of processes, as well as an Eulerian representation via an adapted continuity equation, extending classical results of Wasserstein spaces to the adapted setting. Moreover, we characterize geodesics in this space, and from this derive an adapted Benamou-Brenier-type formula. I will then restrict the attention to Gaussian processes, where we can explicitly describe the solutions to the adapted Wasserstein transport, as well as the geodesics and the tangent space. Based on joint works with D. Bartl, A. Grass, S. Hou, D. Krsek, G. Pammer, M. Rodrigues, S. Schrott.
entries.bio: Beatrice Acciaio is an Associate Professor of Mathematics at ETH Zurich. Her research interests include stochastic processes, optimal transport, mathematical finance, and probability theory.

entries.seminar_title: Coupled Semilinear Stochastic Evolution Equations and LQ Mean Field Games in Hilbert Spaces: Cases with and without Common Noise
entries.speaker: Prof. Dena Firoozi
entries.abstract: We first establish the well-posedness of a system of N coupled semilinear stochastic evolution equations, laying the foundation for mean-field games (MFGs) in Hilbert spaces. We then specialize to N-player linear–quadratic (LQ) games and study the asymptotic behavior as the number of agents N tends to infinity. An infinite-dimensional variant of the Nash Certainty Equivalence (NCE) principle is developed and a unique Nash equilibrium for the limiting MFG is characterized. We show that the corresponding limiting best-response strategies constitute an ϵ-Nash equilibrium for the N-player game in Hilbert spaces. Finally, we extend these results to include an infinite-dimensional common noise. In this setting, the mean-field consistency condition is represented by a system of forward–backward stochastic evolution equations, while in the absence of common noise, it reduces to forward–backward deterministic evolution equations in Hilbert spaces. We establish the solvability of these equations and prove the ϵ-Nash property of the equilibrium strategy in this extended framework.
entries.bio: Dena Firoozi is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Mathematics at the University of Pittsburgh. Her research interests include stochastic differential equations, mean-field games, and optimal control in infinite dimensions.
